reports.title: A Neuromorphic Spiking Neural Network-Based Continual Learning Framework for Energy-Efficient Edge Intelligence in Autonomous UAV Swarm Navigation

identity.excerpt: A Neuromorphic Spiking Neural Network-Based Continual Learning Framework for Energy-Efficient Edge Intelligence in Autonomous UAV Swarm Navigation

architecture.finding: The framework combines onboard event-driven processing, continual adaptation and a graph of UAV peers that share processed representations for local cooperative decisions.

workload.finding: The sensing workload uses event-camera spike streams and a spiking neural network for navigation decisions. The paper evaluates sequential learning tasks in varied scenario types.
workload.original_locator: pp. 5–6 and 9–11, Methodology, Implementation and Results, Table 2

partition_assignment.finding: The design exchanges compact semantic or graph representations among neighbors; it does not present collaborative execution by splitting contiguous neural layers.
partition_assignment.original_locator: pp. 7–8 and 12, Methodology and Scalability Analysis

optimization.finding: The paper describes continual learning with replay and weight consolidation, graph-based coordination and a reinforcement-learning objective for navigation.
optimization.original_locator: pp. 6–9, Methodology and Implementation and Results

compute_radio.finding: The study describes low-power edge compute and names software components and simulators. The reporting does not fully specify the onboard compute and radio configuration of each comparative result.
compute_radio.original_locator: pp. 5–9, Methodology and Implementation and Results

mobility_continuity.finding: Environmental and communication changes are considered in the design and scenario descriptions. Fully specified link interruption and recovery measurement conditions are not provided for the reported comparisons.
mobility_continuity.original_locator: pp. 8–10 and 12, Methodology and Implementation and Results

evaluation.finding: The authors report simulated swarm experiments and describe hardware-in-the-loop activity on embedded platforms. The text does not identify how every tabulated outcome maps to the two evaluation modes.

baselines.finding: Table 1 presents CNN, vision-transformer and conventional SNN alternatives. Table 4 compares components of the proposed stack in an ablation.

outcomes.finding: The tables report navigation, continual retention, scalability and component outcomes. This review retains qualitative categories because correspondence between reported measures, implementation modality and matched conditions is incomplete.

variability.finding: The report varies scenario, learning task, swarm scale and ablative configuration. The inspected Methods and comparative results do not state independent repeated-run counts or uncertainty intervals.

code_data.finding: No exact study code or data release is identified in the implementation sections, conclusion and end matter. Named third-party frameworks do not establish release of this study.
code_data.original_locator: pp. 9 and 14–17, Implementation and Results, Conclusion and References

funding_conflicts.finding: The inspected first page, conclusion and end matter contain no explicit study funding or competing-interest statement.
funding_conflicts.original_locator: pp. 1 and 14–17, first page and end matter

limitations.finding: The authors identify further dynamic edge and multimodal extensions. A dedicated discussion tracing limitations of the reported evaluations is not given in the inspected conclusion.
limitations.original_locator: pp. 14–16, Conclusion and future research paragraph

reports.title: NetMoE: Joint Trajectory Planning and Distributed Mixture-of-Experts Inference for UAV Swarms

identity.excerpt: NetMoE: Joint Trajectory Planning and Distributed Mixture-of-Experts Inference for UAV Swarms

architecture.finding: An airborne swarm hosts distributed expert components. A hierarchical design coordinates software control and expert assignment. The study also evaluates a decentralized control alternative.

workload.finding: The study models a mixture-of-experts inference workload with task and expert compatibility. The nominal simulator abstracts inference into inputs. The measured-gate subexperiment uses a CIFAR-100 classifier instantiation; this is not an airborne deployment.
workload.original_locator: pp. 4–5, 9–11 and 17, §§III.C–D, VI.A–B, measured-gate experiment and VII

partition_assignment.finding: Different UAV nodes host different expert components, and inference is assigned to suitable experts. An evaluation contrasts the expert assignment unit with layer-wise inference.
partition_assignment.original_locator: pp. 4, 6–8 and 12, §§III.C, V.B–D and Table V

optimization.finding: The method combines control and expert assignment under latency and communication constraints. A learned decision component is compared with alternative decision rules.

compute_radio.finding: The study parameterizes node compute and models wireless communication, interference and deployment resource accounting. The modeled assumptions are not physical radio or compute measurements.

mobility_continuity.finding: Software evaluations vary network and mobility conditions, including disrupted connectivity. Some alternative conditions are sensitivity tests under the trained design rather than airborne recovery tests.

evaluation.finding: The study uses a software evaluation with multiple seeds and episodes. Physical validation is deferred by the authors.

baselines.finding: The evaluation compares layer-wise execution, candidate routing and control rules, and ablated configurations. Conditions are separately fixed for different comparison tables.

outcomes.finding: Completion, latency and resource use are reported in simulation. Interpret results by comparison table and operating condition; the review does not extend them to real flight.

variability.finding: The paper reports three-seed evaluation and many episodes, uncertainty intervals, component ablations and sensitivity to modeled conditions.

code_data.finding: The authors provide the code and simulation environment route github.com/traumasv/NetMoE-IoTJ in a source footnote. Review verification establishes the printed route.

funding_conflicts.finding: The Acknowledgment discloses grant support. The inspected first page and end matter do not give a separate competing-interest statement.
funding_conflicts.original_locator: pp. 1 and 17–18, first page and Acknowledgment

limitations.finding: The authors bound the evidence to simulation, discrete motion, abstracted expert accuracy and future real-testbed validation.

reports.title: UAV Extreme Edge Computing for Real Time AI Inference: A Distributed Processing Approach

identity.excerpt: UAV Extreme Edge Computing for Real Time AI Inference: A Distributed Processing Approach

architecture.finding: An orchestrator divides video frames among parallel inference workers and recombines their detections. Worker roles are implemented as workstation processes standing in for UAV devices.

workload.finding: YOLO11m exported to ONNX evaluates urban surveillance video. The video content and resolution are described; the original video source is not identified in the inspected setup.

partition_assignment.finding: The system divides input frames spatially with controlled overlap, performs worker-local inference and merges globally mapped detections.

optimization.finding: The implementation assigns worker threads and frame regions and evaluates adaptive thread reallocation and heterogeneous allocation. The system is evaluated as a parallel implementation on a workstation.

compute_radio.finding: The implementation documents an AMD workstation and HTTP/JPEG data transfer. The evaluation lacks measured airborne wireless links; the authors identify sensitivity to the link bandwidth.

mobility_continuity.finding: The paper describes replacement of stateless workers and tests changing thread allocations on a workstation. It does not demonstrate interference, flight motion or real link-disconnection recovery.

evaluation.finding: Inference measurements use workstation processes with varying computational allocations to emulate UAV workers. The platform and video workload are stated in §III.D.

baselines.finding: Evaluation reports single-worker baselines, parallel worker counts, ideal throughput scaling and comparisons among different resource allocations.

outcomes.finding: Measured workstation outcomes include frame latency, throughput, detection quality and communication overhead; the evidence is specific to the emulated resource setup.

variability.finding: The authors show per-frame latency distribution, scaling and heterogeneity sweeps. The inspected setup/results do not establish independent run counts or outcome confidence intervals.

code_data.finding: The report identifies implementation components and describes workload footage. A release for study source code, raw video or traces is not stated in the inspected sections.

funding_conflicts.finding: The Acknowledgment names Canadian natural sciences and engineering research council support. No competing-interest statement is identified in inspected end matter.

limitations.finding: The authors state that transfer latency depends on inter-node bandwidth and would increase under constrained wireless conditions, limiting how workstation timing generalizes.

quantitative_rows.denominator: throughput units; independent repeat count not stated
quantitative_rows.workload: video frame object detection with YOLO11m on the workload in §III.D
quantitative_rows.conditions: four worker processes, four threads each, versus one four-thread process on the same workstation; aggregate processing resources increase
quantitative_rows.locator: Table I, Threads=4; §IV.B paragraph reporting 22.4 FPS and Fig. 1 caption

reports.title: MARL-based Reliability-aware Video Analytics in Multi-UAV-Assisted MEC Systems

identity.excerpt: MARL-based Reliability-aware Video Analytics in Multi-UAV-Assisted MEC Systems

architecture.finding: UAVs analyze video locally or collaborate with edge computing resources. The reliability-aware method coordinates choices among UAVs and the edge.

workload.finding: Evaluation uses urban traffic video and object-detection CNN configurations at multiple resolutions. Request patterns are derived separately from an external usage distribution.

partition_assignment.finding: Per-task decisions select local or remote execution and model/input configurations. This is task-level allocation, with no consecutive-layer split.

optimization.finding: A multi-agent learner jointly addresses inference configuration and offloading and incorporates computation or transmission failures in the reliability model.

compute_radio.finding: Physical UAV and edge hardware are profiled. The training model uses probabilistic path loss and communication effects. Profile measurements and modeled links have different provenance.

mobility_continuity.finding: Evaluation accounts for compute and link reliability using modeled disturbances. The source distinguishes profiling and physical policy deployment from a simulated link; it does not establish an airborne outage experiment.

evaluation.finding: The authors describe actual inference profile measurements and physical multi-UAV policy deployment, as well as offline training and modeled evaluation conditions. Modality depends on the reported result.

baselines.finding: Comparisons include MARL-based analytics, single-node optimization and alternative policies. Ablations serve distinct comparisons.

outcomes.finding: The paper reports analytics accuracy and reliability-related outcomes. Measured model profiles in Tables II–IV are distinct from modeled system-level comparisons.

variability.finding: Training episodes, operating-factor changes and ablations are reported. Independent repeats and run-level uncertainty are not established by the inspected evaluation.

code_data.finding: The article cites video material and a request-pattern proxy. A study code or experiment trace release is not identified in the inspected text.

funding_conflicts.finding: The study discloses grant support. The inspected first page and end matter lack a competing-interest declaration.
funding_conflicts.original_locator: pp. 1 and 13, first page and end matter

limitations.finding: The authors identify incomplete modeling of scheduling jitter and battery voltage, and defer dedicated fault-injection validation.

reports.title: LLM-based UAV Path Planning for Autonomous and Adaptive Industry Systems

identity.excerpt: LLM-based UAV Path Planning for Autonomous and Adaptive Industry Systems

architecture.finding: Small models serve edge roles and a larger model serves the cloud role. The architecture can revisit selected local inference cases.

workload.finding: Fine-tuned language models process generated multi-UAV decision tasks. The evaluation uses separate training and test samples.

partition_assignment.finding: Work is distributed between edge and cloud models at task level. Replay can revise prior inferences.

optimization.finding: The study describes generated fine-tuning samples, model selection and a scene memory/replay component for simulated edge–cloud coordination and model evaluation.

compute_radio.finding: A lab server and software versions are given, alongside modeled system and communication conditions. Device-side roles are represented in software.

mobility_continuity.finding: Motion and decisions are simulated. Replay addresses inference errors; no actual network outage recovery validation is identified.

evaluation.finding: Experiments use a lab server and generated gridded simulation settings. Local and cloud labels are experimental roles.

baselines.finding: Comparisons distinguish language models, edge-only or cloud-only and coordinated inference, and heuristic and DRL task-planning baselines.

outcomes.finding: The software results report task completion, processing time and system cost. Each comparison applies to its own workload and baseline group.

variability.finding: Scenario variants and comparative conditions are reported. Outcome uncertainty intervals and independent seed replication are not specified for the inspected comparisons.

code_data.finding: The authors describe internal data generation and software dependencies. No release of the study dataset or implementation is identified in the inspected text.

funding_conflicts.finding: A first-page footnote declares grants. The inspected first page and final pre-reference text lack a competing-interest statement.

limitations.finding: The discussion and conclusion identify inference resource costs and the need for improved resilience and broader collaboration.

reports.title: Outdoor Multi-UAV Collaborative Task Planning System Based on Multi-Agent and Improved PPO Algorithm

identity.excerpt: Outdoor Multi-UAV Collaborative Task Planning System Based on Multi-Agent and Improved PPO Algorithm

architecture.finding: A shared language model decomposes tasks across simulated UAV agents. Perception feedback informs the common task graph.

workload.finding: The evaluation includes multi-agent planning and perception-plus-planning scenarios in Microsoft AirSim.

partition_assignment.finding: A controller decomposes and updates shared tasks, using feedback from the agents. This is task-level sequencing and assignment rather than layer partition.

optimization.finding: The paper presents a multi-agent policy variant and task-graph rules. It compares the planning component separately from scenario demonstrations.

compute_radio.finding: The study names workstation and software components. No physical compute or radio measurements across UAV devices are reported in the experimental setup.

mobility_continuity.finding: Simulated scenes vary obstacles and coordination. The inspected results do not describe a measured airborne outage or recovery test.

evaluation.finding: The authors identify workstation software experiments using Microsoft AirSim and comparisons implemented in MATLAB. Scene descriptions do not establish field flight.

baselines.finding: Table 1 contrasts planning policies under agent and obstacle settings. Table 2 instead contrasts coordination architectures. Neither measures standalone neural inference latency.

outcomes.finding: The evaluation reports path length, planning-step time and success, plus separate plan-response time, task completion time and success for coordination experiments.

variability.finding: Scenarios and group size vary. The coordination tasks were each run at least 30 times as reported. Independent seeding and uncertainty intervals are not specified.

code_data.finding: AirSim scenes and software tools are named. No study implementation or task-prompt release is identified. The authors explicitly note the prompts are omitted.

funding_conflicts.finding: No study funding or competing-interest declaration is identified in the inspected first page and end sections.
funding_conflicts.original_locator: pp. 1 and 5–6, first page and end matter

limitations.finding: The authors note omitted scenario prompts and identify future work in the conclusion.

reports.title: Continuous Marine Monitoring via Autonomous UAV Handoff

identity.excerpt: Continuous Marine Tracking via Autonomous UAV Handoff

architecture.finding: The design coordinates two UAV tracking roles and transfers tracking information so a receiving UAV can continue monitoring.

workload.finding: The tracker comparison uses a custom set of aerial marine footage, with changing views, partial occlusion and background noise.

partition_assignment.finding: Handoff exchanges tracking state at task level. Matching and onboard tracking are separate from neural-layer partition.

optimization.finding: The study describes tracker selection, feature matching, template padding and onboard implementation optimization. It tests configuration alternatives rather than an offloading optimizer.

compute_radio.finding: The design names onboard Jetson and ROS/flight-stack integration and Wi-Fi transfer. Power and compute measures refer to the reported HIL operation.

mobility_continuity.finding: The design addresses planned handoff of monitoring. Validation tests tracking and feature matching, and explicitly identifies the onboard system test as hardware-in-the-loop.

evaluation.finding: The study compares trackers on recorded footage and reports hardware-in-the-loop operation including tracking, matching, coordination and navigation logic.

baselines.finding: Tracker alternatives are compared on marine footage. The handoff experiment varies template padding to assess matching separately.

outcomes.finding: Results cover tracking accuracy, matching coverage and persistence, and onboard rate, power and compute behavior. Footage and HIL results support different claims.

variability.finding: The evaluation varies tracker and matching settings. It does not specify independent mission repetitions or uncertainty for the handoff outcomes.

code_data.finding: The authors describe a custom footage dataset and named trackers. The inspected text does not identify a release for study data, coordination code or HIL configuration.

funding_conflicts.finding: No study funding or competing-interest declaration is identified in the inspected first page and end matter.
funding_conflicts.original_locator: pp. 1 and 6, first page, conclusion and References

limitations.finding: The authors note differing viewpoints and incomplete bounding-box alignment in the matching results. There is no dedicated limitations discussion in the conclusion.

quantitative_rows.metric: target coverage in handoff template matching
quantitative_rows.denominator: author-reported Target Cover percentage; underlying independent run count is not specified in Table 3
quantitative_rows.workload: same report’s handoff matching evaluation on marine imagery
quantitative_rows.conditions: 70-pixel versus 30-pixel template padding; matching coverage rather than end-to-end flight handoff success
quantitative_rows.locator: §5.2, Table 3, 70 and 30 padding rows, Target Cover column
